Statistical tests for Markov chains

Source: R/statisticalTests.R
statisticalTests.Rd

Tests of hypotheses on observed sequences of states, based on transition counts (Anderson and Goodman 1957; Kullback, Kupperman and Ku 1962):

  • verifyMarkovProperty(): the first-order Markov property, i.e. that the next state is independent of the previous one given the present one (against a second-order chain);

  • assessOrder(): the same hypothesis with the Pearson statistic, also for a list of independent sequences;

  • verifyEmpiricalToTheoretical(): that the sequence (or a matrix of transition counts) comes from a given chain;

  • verifyHomogeneity(): that several sequences (or count matrices) share the same transition matrix;

  • assessStationarity(): that the transition probabilities do not change over time, comparing nblocks consecutive blocks of the sequence.

Usage

verifyMarkovProperty(
  sequence,
  method = c("G", "Pearson", "simulation"),
  B = 9999,
  seed = NULL,
  verbose = TRUE
)

assessOrder(sequence, verbose = TRUE)

verifyEmpiricalToTheoretical(
  data,
  object,
  method = c("G", "Pearson", "simulation"),
  B = 9999,
  seed = NULL,
  verbose = TRUE
)

verifyHomogeneity(
  inputList,
  method = c("G", "Pearson", "simulation"),
  B = 9999,
  seed = NULL,
  verbose = TRUE
)

assessStationarity(sequence, nblocks, structural.zeros = NULL, verbose = TRUE)

Arguments

sequence

An observed sequence of states (a vector); for assessOrder() also a list of independent sequences, whose triples of consecutive states are formed within each sequence and pooled.

method

The statistic: "G" (likelihood ratio, the default), "Pearson", or "simulation" (likelihood ratio with a Monte Carlo p-value).

B

Number of Monte Carlo samples for method = "simulation".

seed

Optional random seed for method = "simulation".

verbose

Logical: print the result?

data

An observed sequence of states, or a matrix of transition counts with the states as dimnames.

object

A markovchain object, the chain of the null hypothesis.

inputList

A list of at least two observed sequences or matrices of transition counts (with the states as dimnames).

nblocks

Number of consecutive blocks of (nearly) equal length into which the sequence is split, at least two.

structural.zeros

Optional logical matrix, with one row and column per state (in the order of unique(sequence), or with the states as dimnames), marking the transitions that are impossible; they are left out of the comparison.

Value

An object of class "htest", printed if verbose = TRUE and returned invisibly, with the usual components statistic, parameter (degrees of freedom), p.value, method and data.name, and also dof. Depending on the test it also contains the observed and expected counts and the estimated transitionMatrix (verifyMarkovProperty(), verifyEmpiricalToTheoretical()), the pooled counts and the transitionCounts of each element (verifyHomogeneity()), and, with method = "simulation", the simulated statistics (simulations) and B.

Details

Each test compares observed transition counts with the counts expected under the null hypothesis, by the likelihood-ratio statistic \(G^2 = 2 \sum O \log(O / E)\) (method = "G") or by Pearson's \(X^2 = \sum (O - E)^2 / E\) (method = "Pearson"); cells with no expected count are left out, and the degrees of freedom count only the transitions actually observed. The p-value is from the chi-squared distribution, or, with method = "simulation", from B samples simulated under the null hypothesis (the \(G^2\) statistic, p-value \((1 + \#\{simulated \ge observed\}) / (B + 1)\)), which is more reliable when many counts are small. Sequences of numbers or factors are compared as character strings.

References

Anderson, T. W. and Goodman, L. A. (1957). Statistical inference about Markov chains. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 28(1), 89-110.

Kullback, S., Kupperman, M. and Ku, H. H. (1962). Tests for contingency tables and Markov chains. Technometrics 4(4), 573-608.

See also

assessIndependence() (independence of consecutive states), selectOrder() (order by information criteria), compareChains().

Examples

data(rain, package = "markovchain")
# first-order Markov property of the Alofi rainfall sequence
verifyMarkovProperty(rain$rain)
#> 
#> 	Likelihood-ratio test
#> 
#> data:  rain$rain
#> G-squared = 25.837, df = 12, p-value = 0.01132
#> 
assessOrder(rain$rain)
#> 
#> 	Pearson's Chi-squared test for Markov order
#> 
#> data:  rain$rain
#> X-squared = 26.096, df = 12, p-value = 0.0104
#> 

# compatibility with a chain: the fitted one, and a different one
fit <- markovchainFit(rain$rain)$estimate
verifyEmpiricalToTheoretical(rain$rain, fit)
#> 
#> 	Likelihood-ratio test
#> 
#> data:  rain$rain
#> G-squared = 0, df = 6, p-value = 1
#> 
s <- c("0", "1-5", "6+")
uniform <- new("markovchain", states = s,
               transitionMatrix = matrix(1 / 3, 3, 3, dimnames = list(s, s)))
verifyEmpiricalToTheoretical(rain$rain, uniform)
#> 
#> 	Likelihood-ratio test
#> 
#> data:  rain$rain
#> G-squared = 325.12, df = 6, p-value < 2.2e-16
#> 

# the first and second half of the sequence have the same transitions
verifyHomogeneity(list(rain$rain[1:548], rain$rain[549:1096]))
#> 
#> 	Likelihood-ratio test
#> 
#> data:  list(rain$rain[1:548], rain$rain[549:1096])
#> G-squared = 11.231, df = 6, p-value = 0.0815
#> 
# time-homogeneity over four blocks
assessStationarity(rain$rain, nblocks = 4)
#> 
#> 	Pearson's Chi-squared test for time-homogeneity
#> 
#> data:  rain$rain
#> X-squared = 29.051, df = 18, p-value = 0.04776
#> 

# a Monte Carlo p-value
verifyMarkovProperty(rain$rain, method = "simulation", B = 499, seed = 1)
#> 
#> 	Parametric Monte Carlo test (likelihood-ratio statistic)
#> 
#> data:  rain$rain
#> G-squared = 25.837, df = 12, p-value = 0.008
#>
